d.g: A Korean stew, typically made with meat, seafood or vegetables in a seasoned broth and served boiling hot.
d.x: This was where my obsession with jjigae began. I set out to learn how to make not only this gateway jjigae, but all of the most popular jjigae of Korean cuisine: sundubu jjigae, kimchi jiigae^([sic]), gochujang jjigae and doenjang jjigae. Chicken soup may be for the soul, but jjigae is comfort food of the highest order.

jjigae.e: Borrowed from Korean 찌개 (jjigae), from 찌- (jji-, “to steam”) + -개 (-gae, suffix denoting something small associated with an action).

d.g: A Korean dish of noodles with a sauce made from black beans.
d.x: It would not be an understatement to say Korean diets would not be the same without this dish – most Koreans eat it regularly, and have their favorite jjajangmyeon delivery shop on speed dial.

jjajangmyeon.e: Borrowed from Korean 짜장면 (jjajangmyeon). Doublet of zhajiangmian.

d.g: A spicy Korean soup with noodles and seafood.

jjamppong.e: Borrowed from Korean 짬뽕 (jjamppong). Doublet of champon.

d.g: A type of Korean traditional bathhouse, typically having hot tubs, showers, saunas, and massage tables.
d.x: Fans of jjimjilbangs will find a brand-new one five-minutes' walk north of the bus terminal, on the same main road.

jjimjilbang.e: Borrowed from Korean 찜질방 (jjimjilbang), from 찜질 (jjimjil, “stupe, poultice, heating”) + 방(房) (bang, “room”).

d.g: The combination of Chapagetti (Nongshim's instant jjajangmyeon) and Neoguri (Nongshim's instant spicy seafood-flavor noodle).

jjapaguri.e: Borrowed from Korean 짜파구리 (jjapaguri); blend of 짜파게티 (jjapageti, “Chapagetti”) + 너구리 (neoguri, “Neoguri”).
